prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: a damaged shed or outbuilding. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 1)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When the loss is to a shed or outbuilding, check whether it is actually insured as part of the main home policy and whether it sits within the declared property boundary, because many disputes come from assumed cover rather than confirmed cover."},{"type":"fact","content":"When damage follows storm conditions, look for a clear link between the weather event and the failure, as a shed that was already tired, rotten or poorly fixed down is usually only partly attributable to the storm."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the roof is affected, I find it helps to separate missing panels, lifted felt and internal water ingress, because minor external damage can hide a bigger problem only if water has been getting in for a while."},{"type":"fact","content":"When an outbuilding contains tools, bikes or garden equipment, I should check whether the contents limit is lower than the main house contents limit, because cover is often capped more tightly for sheds than for the home itself."},{"type":"preference","content":"When photos are available, I prefer close-ups of the fixings, hinges, door frame and roof edges as well as a wider shot, because those details usually show whether the shed failed from impact, wear or poor maintenance."},{"type":"observation","content":"When there is damage to a timber shed after strong winds, I should ask whether the base, anchor points and surrounding fencing were also affected, because movement of the whole structure can matter more than the broken cladding."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the shed is used as a workshop, the contents and any permanent fixtures may need to be treated differently from loose garden items, so I should not assume everything inside is automatically classed the same way."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the claim mentions escape of water from a hose, tank or appliance in an outbuilding, I should check whether the source was within the insured property and whether the damage was sudden rather than long-term seepage."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the repair looks straightforward, I prefer to confirm whether a local repair to doors, felt or a single panel is enough before considering full replacement, because over-replacing a modest shed can exceed what is reasonable under delegated authority."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the outbuilding is unsafe or exposed after the event, I should consider temporary make-safe costs separately from the final repair, because boarding up, tarpaulins or removal of sharp debris are often the most urgent early spend."}]}
